headline: Showers spread across the region overnight into Sunday, with brief heavy downpours possible near the coast and the LA Basin Sunday afternoon (around a quarter inch), a warm, dry Thanksgiving follows, but forecasters have significant concern for moderate to major coastal flooding and big surf during Thanksgiving week.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A few showers have formed along a weakening front in northwestern San Luis Obispo County Saturday evening and are expected to spread across the region overnight into Sunday. Some showers could be stronger near the coast, with brief heavy downpours and totals around a quarter inch, but they should weaken a lot as they move inland, and many interior spots may stay dry. Overnight lows drop into the 30s in the interior, and frost alerts may be needed for the Antelope Valley; there is no marine layer at LAX, and skies at the Burbank and LAX airports should stay mostly clear through Sunday morning, with light northeast breezes possible near LAX overnight.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Showers continue Sunday and Sunday night as the weak storm works south and east, and by Sunday afternoon some heavier ones could reach the Ventura County coast and the LA Basin, including the Glendale area. Most places are likely to get measurable rain, though chances are noticeably lower in the Antelope Valley; totals are mostly a quarter inch or less, with the most in San Luis Obispo County and possibly a bit more right at the coast. High pressure keeps Monday and most of Tuesday dry and cool, with a couple of degrees of warming Sunday and Monday, then a light wind off the land on Tuesday warms highs west of the mountains to the upper 60s to mid 70s. The next storm reaches northern areas late Tuesday, bringing a tenth of an inch or less to San Luis Obispo County by Tuesday evening.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Another weak storm crosses the area Wednesday, with rain chances of 20 percent or less in Los Angeles and Ventura counties and only a few hundredths of an inch if any falls; San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties get the most, a tenth to a quarter inch, and up to three quarters of an inch in northwest San Luis Obispo County. Thanksgiving and Black Friday are warm and dry as high pressure builds overhead, with highs in the 70s west of the mountains (about 4 to 8 degrees above normal) and the 60s inland (2 to 4 degrees above normal). Some winds blowing off the land are expected, especially Friday morning, but the chance of advisory-level winds is under 10 percent. Saturday turns a few degrees cooler as another weak storm brings a chance of light showers, likely under a tenth of an inch.

coast: Forecasters have significant concern for moderate to major coastal flooding during Thanksgiving week, from a combination of unusually high sea levels (warm ocean water expands), very high spring tides and a large, long-period west swell. For the Central Coast, Ventura and Los Angeles county beaches, a Coastal Flood Advisory runs from 3 AM Monday to 3 AM Wednesday, followed by a Coastal Flood Watch from late Tuesday night through Thursday afternoon as the swell arrives; peak high tides come between 8:45 and 10 AM at roughly 8.2–8.4 feet for Los Angeles and Ventura and 7.9–8.2 feet on the Central Coast, with a reasonable worst case 0.3–0.5 feet higher, and significant impacts seem probable. If upgraded to a warning, flooding could reach farther inland and damage coastal roads and buildings, with significant beach erosion; areas of greatest concern include Santa Monica to Palos Verdes, Long Beach/Naples, Faria to Silver Strand Beach including Ventura Harbor, and Morro Bay, Pismo Beach, Oceano Dunes and the Cayucos, Avila and Pismo piers. A High Surf Advisory covers the Central Coast from 6 AM Sunday to 3 PM Thursday: surf up to 11 feet Monday morning, a lull Monday night into Tuesday, then rapid building to 10–15 feet Wednesday morning and 15–20 feet Wednesday afternoon and evening, possibly higher, with an upgrade to a High Surf Warning increasingly likely, probably by Tuesday. Ventura and Los Angeles county beaches see elevated to high surf much of the week, peaking Wednesday and Thursday with likely High Surf Advisories and a small chance of warning-level surf up to 15 feet on the Ventura coast. The Santa Barbara South Coast (Santa Barbara to Rincon and Jalama Beach) and the islands are under a Coastal Flood Advisory from 3 AM Monday to 3 PM Thursday, with more coastal alerts likely Friday. Offshore, winds and seas stay below small craft advisory levels through Tuesday; a significant west swell around 14–16 feet arrives midweek with large, hazardous seas on the outer waters, and advisory-level northwest to west winds are possible Wednesday and Wednesday night south of Point Conception. Officials advise staying off the beach and away from rock jetties, and avoiding flooded roads and walkways.
watch_for: Coastal flooding: the Coastal Flood Watch for Wednesday–Thursday morning high tides (8:45–10 AM) could be upgraded to a warning as the big swell arrives.
High surf of 15–20 feet or more on the Central Coast Wednesday, and possible warning-level surf on the Ventura coast.
Brief heavy downpours near the coast Sunday, which could push rain totals a bit higher there; plus the timing and amount of Wednesday's rain, where computer models disagree a bit.
confidence: Forecasters see no major changes to the week's outlook and computer models broadly agree, though Sunday's coastal rain totals may need to be nudged up; for the coast they say significant flooding impacts seem probable, though exactly how the tides and swell line up is still somewhat uncertain.
